### Problem: a spruce is a tree of leaf-children {#sec-tr-p4-spruce}

::: {.p-statement}
A rooted tree on vertices $1..n$, root $1$. For $i = 2..n$ the parent $p_i$ satisfies $1 \le p_i < i$. The tree is a spruce when every vertex that has children has at least three children that are themselves leaves. Print `Yes` or `No`.

Constraints: $3 \le n \le 1000$.

Source: [CF 913B · Christmas Spruce](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/913/B){.solved rating="1200"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
A vertex is a leaf when nobody names it as a parent. The test looks only at children, not at grandchildren, so two counters are enough: how many children, and how many of those are leaves. The second counter has to wait until every parent has been seen, because children have larger labels than their parent.
:::

::: {#fig-tr-spruce}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):

    root = V.Node("1", [
        V.Node("2", [
            V.Node("5", color="amber"),
            V.Node("6", color="amber"),
            V.Node("7", color="amber"),
        ], color="red"),
        V.Node("3", color="green"),
        V.Node("4", color="green"),
    ])
    V.tree(ax, p, root, dx=1.05, dy=1.3, size=10)

V.show(draw)
```

Parents $1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2$. Leaves are shaded. Vertex $1$ has two leaf-children, and vertex $2$ is a child that is not a leaf, so the tree is not a spruce.

:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Two counters.** Pass 1 counts children. Pass 2, if `children[i] == 0`, adds one leaf-child to the parent. Every vertex with children then needs at least three leaf-children.
2. **Children lists.** The same test, reading the list. This is the form that extends to "the leaf-children have distinct colours", where a counter is not enough.

**Invariant.** After pass 1, `children[v]` is the number of vertices whose stored parent is $v$. A vertex with that count equal to $0$ is a leaf. Pass 2 runs after pass 1 has seen every parent. The root of a spruce is never a leaf: it has children, and it is still tested.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Two counters

::: {.form-next}
$p_i < i$ makes a forward pass safe: when you look at $i$, its parent already exists. Start the leaf pass at $2$, because $p_1$ is not stored.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get('spruce', 'count')
    assert str(final) == 'No'
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def spruce(n, ps):
    """ps is p_2, p_3, ..., p_n."""
    children = [0] * (n + 1)
    leaf_kids = [0] * (n + 1)
    p = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i, pi in enumerate(ps, start=2):
        p[i] = pi
        children[pi] += 1
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        if children[i] == 0:
            leaf_kids[p[i]] += 1
    ok = all(leaf_kids[v] >= 3 for v in range(1, n + 1) if children[v])
    return "Yes" if ok else "No"
```

##### C++

```cpp
string spruce(int n, const vector<int>& ps) {
    vector<int> children(n + 1), leafKids(n + 1), p(n + 1);
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; ++i) {
        p[i] = ps[i - 2];
        ++children[p[i]];
    }
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; ++i)
        if (children[i] == 0) ++leafKids[p[i]];
    for (int v = 1; v <= n; ++v)
        if (children[v] && leafKids[v] < 3) return "No";
    return "Yes";
}
```

:::

#### Children lists

::: {.form-next}
Store the children, then count how many of them have an empty list. A vertex with an empty list is a leaf and is skipped.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get('spruce', 'lists')
    assert str(final) == 'No'
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def spruce_lists(n, ps):
    ch = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for i, pi in enumerate(ps, start=2):
        ch[pi].append(i)
    for v in range(1, n + 1):
        if not ch[v]:
            continue
        leaves = sum(1 for c in ch[v] if not ch[c])
        if leaves < 3:
            return "No"
    return "Yes"


assert spruce(4, [1, 1, 1]) == spruce_lists(4, [1, 1, 1]) == "Yes"
assert spruce(7, [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2]) == "No"
assert spruce(8, [1, 1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3]) == "Yes"
```

##### C++

```cpp
string spruceLists(int n, const vector<int>& ps) {
    vector<vector<int>> ch(n + 1);
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; ++i) ch[ps[i - 2]].push_back(i);
    for (int v = 1; v <= n; ++v) {
        if (ch[v].empty()) continue;
        int leaves = 0;
        for (int c : ch[v]) if (ch[c].empty()) ++leaves;
        if (leaves < 3) return "No";
    }
    return "Yes";
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
Both forms are $O(n)$ time and memory. $n \le 1000$, so an $O(n^2)$ scan that asks "is anyone's parent $v$?" for every $v$ also passes. The counters are the ones to keep.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $n = 4$ with three children of the root is `Yes`. Those three children are leaves.
- $n = 7$, parents `1 1 1 2 2 2`: vertex $2$ has three leaf-children, but the root's children are $2, 3, 4$ and only $3$ and $4$ are leaves. `No`.
- Counting every descendant that is a leaf, rather than every child that is a leaf, accepts that second tree. The statement says children.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Counting every child, rather than every child that is a leaf, accepts the drawn tree: the root has three children and one of them is not a leaf.
- A leaf test inside the reading loop runs before that vertex's children have been seen.
- A leaf has no test. Demanding three leaf-children from every vertex, including the leaves, answers No for every tree.
:::

**Variants.** A perfect $k$-ary tree wants every inner vertex to have exactly $k$ children, and one shared leaf depth. A comb wants exactly one leaf-child at each inner vertex. The same test on a pointer tree, restricted to left leaves, is [LC 404 · Sum of Left Leaves](https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-left-leaves/){difficulty="Easy"}.
